query:
Context. We run an AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic atomizer at about 1400 m altitude (room pressure about
850-865 mbar). A charge is induction-melted in a BN-coated graphite crucible; argon over-pressure
("graining" pressure, 0.19 bar on the HMI) pushes the melt through a 0.5 mm hBN nozzle once a stopper
rod is lifted, and the stream falls onto an inclined W-coated carbon-fibre plate driven at 40 kHz
(1:1.5 booster, 90 % amplitude). A "turbo" button applies 1.5 bar while held. Melt the plate does not
atomize is meant to run off into a ceramic catch bowl on the chamber floor. Powder falls through a
water-cooled stainless cone at the bottom of the chamber into a collection container: a glass cylinder
(probably borosilicate; to be confirmed) about 100 mm across, clamped between a stainless top flange
and a stainless bottom plate by four tie rods, inside a perforated steel guard. Elastomer seals
(material not yet known: silicone, FKM or EPDM) seal each end of the glass and the joint between the
cone and the container's top flange. A removable stainless splash disc sits in the top flange. The
chamber is evacuated to about -850 mbar gauge (about 10 mbar absolute) and backfilled with argon
several times, with washes at 250 and 500 C, and runs at about +150 mbar gauge during the pour. An
oxygen sensor reads the chamber gas through a small continuous bleed to the room; its bleed valve is
open only above +50 mbar and closed under vacuum, the display tops out at 1000 ppm, and the reading is
not meaningful under vacuum. Normal runs read the low 20s ppm before the pour and rise to 100-240 ppm
during it.

Alloy: nickel aluminium bronze UNS C63000 (Cu-10Al-5Ni-3Fe wt%; solidus about 1040 C, liquidus about
1054 C), melted at 1300 C (about 245 C superheat). Good runs (Oct 27 and Nov 10, 816-1080 g, new
plate) made fine powder (d50 roughly 100 um) at 75-91 % yield; failed runs (Oct 28, Nov 5) left most
of the charge as a solid puck in the catch bowl or froze in the nozzle. None of those runs damaged the
collection container.

The Nov 13 run (816 g C63000, the Nov 10 plate flipped over to use its other W face, 5 min hold at
1300 C, graining 0.18 bar then 0.19 bar):
1. Before heating, after the first cold purge, the machine was switched off by accident and turned
   back on. From then on the O2 reading sat at its 1000 ppm limit. On the next backfill it fell to
   about 700 ppm, then read 1000 ppm again once the chamber was back at full vacuum. About four extra
   purge cycles did not help. The vacuum only reached about -830 mbar gauge instead of the usual
   -850 mbar, and the operator suspected a small leak at the joint between the cone and the collection
   container (no hiss was heard). The top of the collection container had been taken off two days
   earlier to sample powder. During the pour the HMI read 351 ppm O2 at +142 mbar.
2. The plate scanned and tested normally (one peak at 40.12 kHz; 79 W at 90 % during the pour), but
   it barely atomized: almost all of the charge came off as small shot ("pellets", roughly 1-3 mm)
   with very little powder, and molten bronze piled up on the back wall of the chamber, blackening
   the steel. Bronze fused around the cone's outlet, which has a burnt dark spot at its top edge.
   Video during the pour shows the glass cylinder glowing orange from hot metal inside it.
3. About three quarters of the way through the pour there was a smell of burning rubber, and smoke
   came out of the seal between the cone and the collection container (that is, outward, from the
   overpressured chamber into the room).
4. Afterwards: under a mass of bronze that had piled up at the container's entrance and slid down the
   inside of the glass, a white, crusty, mud-cracked ring about 19 mm tall lined the wall of the
   container's entrance where that seal sits; white powder from it is mixed into the little powder
   that was made. The seal at the bottom of the glass is charred black. The inside of the glass is
   coated with a yellow-brown film, and the glass cylinder has cracked at its top rim, with a piece
   broken out of the edge that sits in the top flange.

Explain this failure and how to prevent it. Give numbers with sources (data sheets, standards, papers
with DOIs) and mark every estimate with its inputs.

1. The seal. For silicone (VMQ), FKM (Viton), EPDM and FFKM seals: continuous and short-term
   temperature limits, how each decomposes in argon with a few hundred ppm O2 versus in air, and what
   each leaves behind (colour, texture, composition). Is a white, cracked, crusty residue the
   signature of silicone turning to silica? Would FKM or EPDM char black instead? What are the
   decomposition products and their hazards (siloxanes and amorphous silica from silicone; HF and
   carbonyl fluoride from FKM above roughly 300-400 C), and how should the residue, the contaminated
   powder and the parts be handled and cleaned?
2. Heat. Estimate the enthalpy of 816 g of C63000 from 1300 C to room temperature (sensible plus
   latent heat). For droplets of 50 um, 200 um, 1 mm and 3 mm falling about 0.5-1 m through argon,
   estimate the time to solidify and the temperature on arrival, and compare fine powder with coarse
   shot and with molten runoff. How hot and how fast would a stainless flange and an elastomer seal
   next to a pile of a few hundred grams of bronze at 900-1050 C get? Why would a run that makes shot
   instead of powder overheat the collection container when good runs and runs that end as a puck in
   the catch bowl do not?
3. The glass. Thermal-shock limits (allowable temperature difference, and the rule of thumb for a
   local hot spot) for soda-lime glass, borosilicate 3.3 and fused quartz, with thickness. Was the
   crack more likely from hot metal touching the glass rim, from the steel flange heating and
   expanding against a clamped rim, or from point loads where the seal burned away? What does a piece
   broken out of the clamped edge indicate? What causes a yellow-brown film on the inside of the glass?
4. Oxygen. Rank the likely causes of the 1000 ppm reading and the 351 ppm during the pour: a real air
   leak at the disturbed collection-container joint (consistent with -830 instead of -850 mbar, or is
   a 20 mbar difference within day-to-day barometric change?), air drawn in or the sensor exposed to
   air when the machine lost power, the sensor's bleed valve being shut under vacuum so room air can
   diffuse back into the sensor, a zirconia cell not yet back at temperature after the power cut, or
   an electrochemical (galvanic) trace sensor saturated by air and slow to recover. How do zirconia
   and electrochemical trace-O2 sensors behave after a power cut and after exposure to air, and how
   long do they take to recover? Give a test that tells a real leak from a sensor fault (for example a
   rate-of-rise test with the pump valved off, soap or helium checks of the clamped joints, and a
   check of the sensor against argon straight from the cylinder).
5. Links between the problems. Could 350-1000 ppm O2 have caused or worsened the failure to atomize
   (Al2O3 skins on a melt with 10 % Al, oxidation of the W coating or carbon fibre, poorer wetting),
   and the seal burning? Could the seal already have been leaking before the run? Separate what the
   evidence supports from what it does not.
6. Prevention, ranked by benefit and cost: a stop rule (abort the pour when the plate makes shot or
   melt piles up); keeping hot metal out of the container (a larger catch bowl, a deflector, or a
   sacrificial metal sleeve or liner protecting the cone outlet, the seal and the top of the glass);
   seal materials and designs suited to occasional hot metal (FFKM, graphite or metal seals, seals set
   back behind a cooled or shielded lip); swapping the glass for fused quartz or an all-metal
   container for copper alloys; a thermocouple on the container's top flange with an alarm; leak
   checks after any part is disturbed; an O2 go/no-go rule (no heating above a set ppm, and what to do
   after a power cut). Include anything known about how other atomizer makers (gas or ultrasonic)
   protect powder collection containers and their seals from hot metal.
task_summary: Analysis Of Ultrasonic Atomizer Failure Causing Seal Decomposition Glass Damage And Preventive Measures

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string encoding an object with an "objectives" list;
never pass objectives separately.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: paper_search
info.description:
Search for papers in Google Scholar for you to look at.

Can be called repeatedly with identical parameters to retrieve more results (max 2 repeats).
A short summary of the retrieved papers will be returned, but to examine the full content of each paper,
you must use the gather_evidence tool.

query.description:
A Google Scholar search query, which can be a specific phrase, complete sentence,
or general keywords, e.g. 'machine learning for immunology'. Also can be
given search operators like 'author:'.
query.title: Query

min_year.description:
filter for minimum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
min_year.title: Min Year

max_year.description:
filter for maximum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
max_year.title: Max Year

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science
        - DEVICE_FEASIBILITY: Device Feasibility
        - OTHER: Other

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions
        - BIOLOGICAL: Biological interventions
        - COMBINATION_PRODUCT: Combination product interventions
        - DEVICE: Device interventions
        - DIAGNOSTIC_TEST: Diagnostic test interventions
        - DIETARY_SUPPLEMENT: Dietary supplement interventions
        - DRUG: Drug interventions
        - GENETIC: Genetic interventions
        - PROCEDURE: Procedure interventions
        - RADIATION: Radiation interventions
        - OTHER: Other interventions

    DesignAllocation:
        - RANDOMIZED: Randomized allocation
        - NON_RANDOMIZED: Non-randomized allocation
        - NA: Not applicable

    InterventionalAssignment:
        - SINGLE_GROUP: Single group assignment
        - PARALLEL: Parallel assignment
        - CROSSOVER: Crossover assignment
        - FACTORIAL: Factorial assignment
        - SEQUENTIAL: Sequential assignment

    ObservationalModel:
        - COHORT: Cohort

    DesignMasking:

    WhoMasked:

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

disease_names.description:
List of disease names to search for.
Usage:

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: Context. We run an AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic atomizer at about 1400 m altitude (room pressure about
850-865 mbar). A charge is induction-melted in a BN-coated graphite crucible; argon over-pressure
("graining" pressure, 0.19 bar on the HMI) pushes the melt through a 0.5 mm hBN nozzle once a stopper
rod is lifted, and the stream falls onto an inclined W-coated carbon-fibre plate driven at 40 kHz
(1:1.5 booster, 90 % amplitude). A "turbo" button applies 1.5 bar while held. Melt the plate does not
atomize is meant to run off into a ceramic catch bowl on the chamber floor. Powder falls through a
water-cooled stainless cone at the bottom of the chamber into a collection container: a glass cylinder
(probably borosilicate; to be confirmed) about 100 mm across, clamped between a stainless top flange
and a stainless bottom plate by four tie rods, inside a perforated steel guard. Elastomer seals
(material not yet known: silicone, FKM or EPDM) seal each end of the glass and the joint between the
cone and the container's top flange. A removable stainless splash disc sits in the top flange. The
chamber is evacuated to about -850 mbar gauge (about 10 mbar absolute) and backfilled with argon
several times, with washes at 250 and 500 C, and runs at about +150 mbar gauge during the pour. An
oxygen sensor reads the chamber gas through a small continuous bleed to the room; its bleed valve is
open only above +50 mbar and closed under vacuum, the display tops out at 1000 ppm, and the reading is
not meaningful under vacuum. Normal runs read the low 20s ppm before the pour and rise to 100-240 ppm
during it.

Alloy: nickel aluminium bronze UNS C63000 (Cu-10Al-5Ni-3Fe wt%; solidus about 1040 C, liquidus about
1054 C), melted at 1300 C (about 245 C superheat). Good runs (Oct 27 and Nov 10, 816-1080 g, new
plate) made fine powder (d50 roughly 100 um) at 75-91 % yield; failed runs (Oct 28, Nov 5) left most
of the charge as a solid puck in the catch bowl or froze in the nozzle. None of those runs damaged the
collection container.

The Nov 13 run (816 g C63000, the Nov 10 plate flipped over to use its other W face, 5 min hold at
1300 C, graining 0.18 bar then 0.19 bar):
1. Before heating, after the first cold purge, the machine was switched off by accident and turned
   back on. From then on the O2 reading sat at its 1000 ppm limit. On the next backfill it fell to
   about 700 ppm, then read 1000 ppm again once the chamber was back at full vacuum. About four extra
   purge cycles did not help. The vacuum only reached about -830 mbar gauge instead of the usual
   -850 mbar, and the operator suspected a small leak at the joint between the cone and the collection
   container (no hiss was heard). The top of the collection container had been taken off two days
   earlier to sample powder. During the pour the HMI read 351 ppm O2 at +142 mbar.
2. The plate scanned and tested normally (one peak at 40.12 kHz; 79 W at 90 % during the pour), but
   it barely atomized: almost all of the charge came off as small shot ("pellets", roughly 1-3 mm)
   with very little powder, and molten bronze piled up on the back wall of the chamber, blackening
   the steel. Bronze fused around the cone's outlet, which has a burnt dark spot at its top edge.
   Video during the pour shows the glass cylinder glowing orange from hot metal inside it.
3. About three quarters of the way through the pour there was a smell of burning rubber, and smoke
   came out of the seal between the cone and the collection container (that is, outward, from the
   overpressured chamber into the room).
4. Afterwards: under a mass of bronze that had piled up at the container's entrance and slid down the
   inside of the glass, a white, crusty, mud-cracked ring about 19 mm tall lined the wall of the
   container's entrance where that seal sits; white powder from it is mixed into the little powder
   that was made. The seal at the bottom of the glass is charred black. The inside of the glass is
   coated with a yellow-brown film, and the glass cylinder has cracked at its top rim, with a piece
   broken out of the edge that sits in the top flange.

Explain this failure and how to prevent it. Give numbers with sources (data sheets, standards, papers
with DOIs) and mark every estimate with its inputs.

1. The seal. For silicone (VMQ), FKM (Viton), EPDM and FFKM seals: continuous and short-term
   temperature limits, how each decomposes in argon with a few hundred ppm O2 versus in air, and what
   each leaves behind (colour, texture, composition). Is a white, cracked, crusty residue the
   signature of silicone turning to silica? Would FKM or EPDM char black instead? What are the
   decomposition products and their hazards (siloxanes and amorphous silica from silicone; HF and
   carbonyl fluoride from FKM above roughly 300-400 C), and how should the residue, the contaminated
   powder and the parts be handled and cleaned?
2. Heat. Estimate the enthalpy of 816 g of C63000 from 1300 C to room temperature (sensible plus
   latent heat). For droplets of 50 um, 200 um, 1 mm and 3 mm falling about 0.5-1 m through argon,
   estimate the time to solidify and the temperature on arrival, and compare fine powder with coarse
   shot and with molten runoff. How hot and how fast would a stainless flange and an elastomer seal
   next to a pile of a few hundred grams of bronze at 900-1050 C get? Why would a run that makes shot
   instead of powder overheat the collection container when good runs and runs that end as a puck in
   the catch bowl do not?
3. The glass. Thermal-shock limits (allowable temperature difference, and the rule of thumb for a
   local hot spot) for soda-lime glass, borosilicate 3.3 and fused quartz, with thickness. Was the
   crack more likely from hot metal touching the glass rim, from the steel flange heating and
   expanding against a clamped rim, or from point loads where the seal burned away? What does a piece
   broken out of the clamped edge indicate? What causes a yellow-brown film on the inside of the glass?
4. Oxygen. Rank the likely causes of the 1000 ppm reading and the 351 ppm during the pour: a real air
   leak at the disturbed collection-container joint (consistent with -830 instead of -850 mbar, or is
   a 20 mbar difference within day-to-day barometric change?), air drawn in or the sensor exposed to
   air when the machine lost power, the sensor's bleed valve being shut under vacuum so room air can
   diffuse back into the sensor, a zirconia cell not yet back at temperature after the power cut, or
   an electrochemical (galvanic) trace sensor saturated by air and slow to recover. How do zirconia
   and electrochemical trace-O2 sensors behave after a power cut and after exposure to air, and how
   long do they take to recover? Give a test that tells a real leak from a sensor fault (for example a
   rate-of-rise test with the pump valved off, soap or helium checks of the clamped joints, and a
   check of the sensor against argon straight from the cylinder).
5. Links between the problems. Could 350-1000 ppm O2 have caused or worsened the failure to atomize
   (Al2O3 skins on a melt with 10 % Al, oxidation of the W coating or carbon fibre, poorer wetting),
   and the seal burning? Could the seal already have been leaking before the run? Separate what the
   evidence supports from what it does not.
6. Prevention, ranked by benefit and cost: a stop rule (abort the pour when the plate makes shot or
   melt piles up); keeping hot metal out of the container (a larger catch bowl, a deflector, or a
   sacrificial metal sleeve or liner protecting the cone outlet, the seal and the top of the glass);
   seal materials and designs suited to occasional hot metal (FFKM, graphite or metal seals, seals set
   back behind a cooled or shielded lip); swapping the glass for fused quartz or an all-metal
   container for copper alloys; a thermocouple on the container's top flange with an alarm; leak
   checks after any part is disturbed; an O2 go/no-go rule (no heating above a set ppm, and what to do
   after a power cut). Include anything known about how other atomizer makers (gas or ultrasonic)
   protect powder collection containers and their seals from hot metal.

In this work, a thermal degradation mechanism of room temperature vulcanized (RTV) phenyl silicone rubber that was vulcanized by different crosslinking agents was discussed. Secondly, the ablation properties of RTV phenyl silicone rubber were studied by the muffle roaster test and FT-IR. Thirdly, thermal stability of the three samples was studied by thermogravimetric (TG) analysis. Finally, to explore the thermal degradation mechanism, the RTV phenyl silicone rubber vulcanized by different crosslinking agents were characterized by TG analysis-mass spectrum (TG-MS) and pyrolysis gas chromatogram-mass spectrum (pyGC-MS). Results showed that the thermal stability of RTV phenyl silicone rubber is related to the amount of residual Si–OH groups. The residual Si–OH groups initiated the polysiloxane chain degradation via an ‘unzipping’ mechanism.

Abstract:
The article illustrates the impact of basalt filler in the form of flakes and fibres on the toxicity of gaseous products that formed during the thermal decomposition of silicone rubber composites. The values of specific emissions of gases were determined with the help of the IR spectroscopy and further applied to calculate the toxicometric index. The presented method of measuring the concentrations of gaseous products resulting from thermal decomposition consists in the application of a fluidised bed reactor, which makes it possible to conduct the decomposition of a sample at a precisely assumed temperature value and imitate the conditions of a real fire. At a temperature lower than 700 °C, the gases resulting from the thermal decomposition of composites are particularly toxic due to the presence of significant concentrations of formaldehyde that does not undergo oxidation to more stable inorganic products. At a temperature of 600 °C the toxicity of gases for the samples with ceramizable additives and without them was similar. In the first case, there appeared to be a positive synergistic effect of mineral and basalt additives, and the basalt additives themselves increased the toxicity of gases. At higher temperatures of decomposition, the exponentially increasing rate of the oxidation reaction in the gaseous phase results in the lack of significant differences between the toxicity of gases for the samples with and without basalt additives. The toxicometric index value at temperatures of 700 °C and 800 °C was by one or two orders of magnitude higher, respectively, than the one that was observed in the temperature range of 500–600 °C, as inorganic components appear in the place of formaldehyde.

Abstract:
Polysilazane and platinum were adopted to enhance the thermal stability of silicone rubber. The effect and mechanism of polysilazane and platinum on enhancing thermal stability were investigated via thermogravimetry, scanning electron microscopy-energy dispersive X-ray spectrometry, thermogravimetry-Fourier transform infrared spectrometry, and Fourier transform infrared spectrometry. Remarkable synergism between polysilazane and platinum was found in enhancing thermal stability of silicone rubber. When 1.34 wt% polysilazane and 8 ppm platinum were added, the degradation temperatures were elevated. Furthermore, the thermal residues of silicone rubbers were increased from 30–45 to 66–76 wt%, and maximum degradation rates were reduced from 8.81–15.8 to 4.55–5.02 wt%/min. Besides, silicone rubber demonstrated excellent shape retention at high temperature in the presence of polysilazane and platinum. The mechanism may be that platinum cooperated with polysilazane and efficiently catalyzed radical crosslinking between polysilazane and silicone chains. As a result, a tightly crosslinked network was developed, and degradation of silicone rubber was suppressed.

Abstract:
<jats:p>This study investigates the pressure-dependent mechanical behavior and surface degradation of fluorocarbon elastomer (FKM, Viton®) O-ring seals following prolonged high-pressure hydrogen exposure. Specimens were aged at up to 7000 psi for 192 h and evaluated using tensile testing and optical image analysis. The results show a non-monotonic evolution of peak force, stiffness, and energy absorption, with increased load-bearing response at higher pressures accompanied by reduced displacement capacity. Normalized force–displacement behavior shows broadly similar loading profiles across pressure conditions; however, this representation is used for comparative visualization and does not establish preservation of the deformation mechanism. Image-based analysis reveals a significant increase in micro-defect density and surface heterogeneity with pressure, suggesting increased formation of surface micro-defects. These findings highlight pressure-dependent changes in polymer network response and surface morphology under hydrogen exposure. The study provides insights into structure–property relationships governing elastomer performance in hydrogen environments.</jats:p>

Abstract:
In the post-processing of large maritime components, a considerable amount of waste in the form of milling and grinding chips is produced. At the same time, additive manufacturing technologies have shown great potential in producing high-volume parts for maritime applications, allowing novel design approaches and short lead times. In this context, this study presents a sustainable approach to recycle and use aluminium bronze waste material, generated during post-processing of large cast ship propellers, as feedstock for laser-powder directed energy deposition. The recycling technology used to produce powder batches is inductive re-melting in combination with ultrasonic atomization. The derived metal powders are characterized using digital image analysis, powder flowability tests, scanning electron microscopy as well as energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy. Compared to conventional metal powders produced by gas atomization, the recycled material shows excellent sphericity and a powder size distribution with a higher content of finer and coarser particles. Metallographic sections of deposited additively produced specimens show an increased hardness and reduced ductility, but also competitive densities and higher yield and ultimate tensile strength compared to cast material. The process chain shows high potential for the maritime sector to enable circular and sustainable manufacturing.

Abstract:
In the manufacturing process of ship propellers, large quantities of grinding chips are generated. These grinding chips result from the finishing of the blade surfaces after the primary casting process of the propeller. The aim of this study was to investigate and compare different preparation processes used to produce chip powders with sufficient powder quality for the additive manufacturing process of directed energy deposition. The preparation of the samples was performed through different sieving, milling and re-melting processes. For the characterization of the prepared samples, powder analysis according to relevant industry standards was carried out. It was found that the re-melting processes result in superior powder quality for additive manufacturing in terms of particle size, morphology, and flowability. For some characteristics, the powder exhibits even better properties than those of commercial powders. Furthermore, the powder properties of the milled samples demonstrate a promising potential for use in additive manufacturing.

Abstract:
Additive manufacturing (AM) has been intensively studied over this decade due to the increasing demand of functional and precise materials in various industries. AM process leverages on the concept of layer by layer deposition or joining of a material at micro‐ or nano‐scale to produce the final products. As such, AM technology is widely used to manufacture products of complex geometries with high precision in a short time. As the quality and the performance of AM manufactured functional products depend on the quality and the cost of the atomized metal or alloy powder used, the use of powders of high size uniformity, high purity, high sphericity, high flowability, low cost, and no trapped gas bubble porosity is necessary. To this end, various metal production technologies were investigated and one of the popular technologies is atomization. This article reviewed the working principles of the various atomization technologies for the production of fine metal and alloy powders. The key atomization conditions discussed in this article include atomization type, material feed rate and temperature, atomizing fluid flow rate, type and temperature, cooling rate, and atomization pressure. In addition, several outlooks on the prospect and the optimization of atomization technologies were also discussed in this article.

Abstract:
The article presents the results of the development works and research on the atomization process carried out using two prototype high-power ultrasonic systems. Ultrasonic systems have been designed to develop a new metal powder production process; these materials are increasingly used in modern manufacturing processes such as additive technologies or spraying and surfacing processes. The preliminary studies presented in the article were conducted for water to assess the effectiveness of both systems and to verify the theoretical and structural assumptions. In ultrasonic atomization, the ultrasonic wave causes the phenomenon of cavitation, which leads to the overcoming of the surface tension forces of the liquid and its disintegration into fine droplets. The important parameters that affect the properties of the produced droplets include, among others, the frequency of the sonotrode vibrations and the amplitude of the vibrations of the working plate. As part of the research, the paper presents the process of selecting the sonotrode geometry for two different values of the transducer’s natural frequencies (20 kHz and 70 kHz). In the design process, the finite element method was used to perform a harmonic analysis and develop the geometry of the sonotrode and the working plate. The design assumptions and the design process were presented. The modeled and then ultrasonic waveguides were verified experimentally by measuring the deflection distribution on the working plate surface using a high-precision laser displacement sensor. Then, the work ultimately resulted in conducting atomization tests of water. The obtained aerosols and the mechanism of their formation were studied using a high-speed camera. Finally, using Matlab R2020a software and image analysis scripts, it was possible to analyze the droplet size distribution generated by both systems. It was observed that 50% of the produced droplets were in the range of 35–55 μm for a 20 kHz system, while for a 70 kHz system it was 10–25 μm, which is a very satisfying distribution in terms of metal powder atomization.

Abstract:
This paper presents the results of a study on the atomisation process of 316L material. The primary objective of the study was to obtain the highest quality, quantity and yield of 316L metal powder for the established atomisation parameters (torch current and wire feed speed) at the assumed process time. Using experiment planning according to the Taguchi method, 16 pairs of controllable variable parameters were developed. It was observed that the low current high-wire speed configuration resulted in the formation of a considerable amount of molten metal on the sonotrode platform. This phenomenon prevented the ultrasound system from working properly, so some of the processes were interrupted. The results obtained from the tests showed that torch current and wire feed speed are parameters that have a significant impact on the efficiency of the ultrasonic atomisation process. The highest efficiency was achieved by the process with a torch current of 100 A and a wire feed speed of 9 mm/s.

Abstract:
Nickel aluminium bronze (NAB) alloys are known for their excellent strength and corrosion resistance, making them suitable for maritime and industrial applications. NAB is producible by Powder Metallurgy (PM) but typically requires high compaction pressure. The objective of this study is to investigate the manufacturing of NAB using the cold spray additive manufacturing (AM) process and to compare its properties to those produced by traditional methods such as casting and PM. Cold spray is a solid-state coating technique that accelerates powdered metal and carrier gas to supersonic speeds, enabling bonding through plastic deformation. Binary aluminium bronze (AB) and NAB alloys were produced using powders by cold spraying powders into 3D printed parts, and heat treating the resulting parts. The AB alloy contained blended 9.9% aluminium alloy (Al6061) powder and copper powder, while the NAB alloy included 11% Al6061 powder, 5.8% nickel powder, 6.8% iron powder, and copper powder. Powders were mixed under controlled conditions and deposited using a LightSPEE3D printer and compressed air. Post-deposition heat treatments, such as homogenisation, aging, and/or hot isostatic pressing (HIP), were applied to enhance material properties. The results indicate that the cold spray process, combined with appropriate heat treatments, can produce NAB alloys with desirable microstructures containing fine κ phases and mechanical properties with above 280 MPa yield strength, above 500 MPa tensile strength and 20% elongation which are comparable to those achieved by traditional cast methods which yield strength of 240 MPa, tensile strength of 580 MPa and 15% elongation, and superior to PM methods. This study demonstrates the viability of cold spray AM to enhance the production of complex high-strength alloys, offering significant advancements for maritime and industrial applications.

The resulting samples were characterized using a suite of complementary techniques, including x-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, energy-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy, nanoindentation, x-ray computed tomography, and electron backscatter diffraction. The as-fabricated microstructures were observed to deviate significantly from typical as-cast configurations. In the AM RGO-coated NAB specimens, the formation of the κI phase was notably suppressed and is attributed to the rapid cooling rates inherent to the AM process. Comparatively, the AM RGO-coated NAB samples exhibited a more refined microstructure with a significantly reduced volume fraction of intermetallic particles compared to their cast NAB and uncoated AM-NAB counterparts. Mechanical assessment through nanoindentation revealed that the RGO-coated parts possess a higher modulus and hardness relative to cast NAB, with an enhancement of over 30%. These enhancements in mechanical properties are attributed to the microstructural advantages conferred by AM processes, including diminished segregation, uniform precipitation distribution, and reduced grain size.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Hydrogen gas sensors are essential for ensuring safety and efficient operation in the expanding hydrogen energy economy and its infrastructure. However, real-world sensor performance is frequently compromised by interference from coexisting gases, environmental fluctuations, and physical disturbances, leading to false alarms, missed detections, and increased recalibration or maintenance burden. This comprehensive review systematically summarizes recent advances in anti-interference technologies for hydrogen gas sensors across material-, signal-processing-, and system-level domains. At the material level, strategies such as noble-metal doping, nanostructure engineering, and selective membrane coatings improve selectivity and long-term stability. At the signal level, advanced noise reduction, dynamic calibration, drift compensation, and machine-learning-based pattern recognition enhance detection accuracy and robustness under varying conditions. At the system level, sensor arrays, optimized packaging, structural isolation, and adaptive redundancy mitigate interference in realistic deployments. By critically evaluating these multi-scale strategies, this review highlights progress, identifies key performance trade-offs, and outlines research directions toward interference-resilient sensing that supports scalable, low-maintenance, and energy-efficient hydrogen infrastructure.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Sensor stability is defined as the ability to maintain a relatively stable and repeatable signal over a sufficient period. Long-term stability for gas sensors is an essential capability for carrying out long-term data collection of human exhaled breath, environmental monitoring and other gas detection in the modern electronic information age. This article reviews the research advances on the stability of metal oxide semiconductor gas sensors in the past five years. The impact of structure, environment, toxicity and sensor array on the sensor stability are discussed. Then, the improvement schemes of existing materials and structure design are summarized. The achievements of structure doping, humidity, anti-poisoning and photoactivation are overviewed. Finally, the great significance of elucidating the sensing mechanism and carrying out the life acceleration test for future research and development is pointed out.

Abstract:
This paper takes the Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer (EPDM) insulation layer of 220kV integral prefabricated cable joint as the research object, performs accelerated thermal aging experiments at 130°C, 145°C, and 160°C, and then conducted Fourier Transform Infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), Thermogravimetric Analysis (TGA) and power frequency breakdown strength test successively. The experimental results show that thermal aging results in long molecular chain degradation, bond breaking and oxidation of EPDM.The initial decomposition temperature decreases gradually with the aging time and the thermal stability decreases gradually under the action of thermal aging. The breakdown field strength decreased by 13.3%, 21.2% and 22.5% respectively at the end of thermal aging, and the decline rate increased with the aging temperature. The main reasons for the decrease of breakdown strength are the precipitation of crosslinking agent, the breaking down of molecular chain and the generation of oxygen-containing groups.

function.arguments: {"question": "What are the thermal decomposition products, temperature limits, and residue characteristics of silicone rubber (VMQ/PDMS) in inert atmosphere (argon)? Does silicone decompose to white silica residue?"}

messages.content:
Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000000

From text 'chen2021synergisticeffectand pages 3-7'.

Wanjuan Chen, Xueyi Zhang, Caiying Liang, Dongchu Chen, Min Zhang, and Lei Miao. Synergistic effect and mechanism of polysilazane and platinum on the thermal stability of silicone rubber. Journal of Elastomers & Plastics, 54:359-373, Sep 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1177/00952443211038675, doi:10.1177/00952443211038675. This article has 3 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt reports thermogravimetric behavior under flowing nitrogen, which is an inert atmosphere comparable to argon, but it does not explicitly identify the volatile decomposition products. Testing was performed from 40 to 800 °C at 20 °C/min. For unmodified silicone rubber (SR/VMQ/PDMS), the temperature for 10% mass loss was 533 °C and that for 20% mass loss was 568 °C; approximately 30 wt% residue remained at 800 °C. Adding PSiN and platinum substantially increased stability: SR/Pt/PSiN had T10 = 567 °C, T20 = 657 °C, and 66 wt% residue at 800 °C. The paper states that SR and SR/PSiN formed white ash after heating to 600–800 °C. However, this should not be interpreted as proof that the residue is pure silica. EDX analysis of the SR residue gave approximately 70.09 atomic% oxygen, 22.09% silicon, and 7.83% carbon, indicating a silica-rich/oxidized inorganic residue retaining carbon and not pure SiO2. The untreated SR residue was loose and porous, whereas the Pt/PSiN-containing residue was compact and continuous. The supplied excerpt does not provide a detailed chemical analysis of gaseous products or an exact terminal decomposition temperature.


---

## pqac-00000001

From text 'he2018howthecrosslinking pages 7-11'.

Chen He, Boqian Li, Ying-Ke Ren, Wu Lu, Yibing Zeng, Wei‐dong He, and Anchao Feng. How the crosslinking agent influences the thermal stability of rtv phenyl silicone rubber. Materials, 12:88, Dec 2018. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/ma12010088, doi:10.3390/ma12010088. This article has 60 citations.

The excerpt describes thermal decomposition of phenyl-containing RTV silicone rubber, rather than unfilled VMQ/PDMS specifically, and it does not state that the experiments were conducted under argon. For TEOS- and TPOS-cured material, decomposition is divided into three stages: an initial approximately 190–320 °C stage attributed mainly to cyclosiloxane oligomer impurities; a 320–480 °C stage involving polymer-chain pyrolysis; and a final 480–630 °C stage. Detected decomposition products include cyclic siloxanes—hexamethylcyclotrisiloxane, octamethylcyclotetrasiloxane, and diphenyltetramethylcyclotrisiloxane—as well as methane and benzene from side-group crosslinking. PyGC-MS at about 700 °C additionally detected methane, benzene, and cyclosiloxanes with methyl or phenyl substituents. Polysilazane-cured rubber showed only two stages, approximately 190–320 °C and 480–630 °C, with maximum degradation near 580 °C and a reported residue rate of 26%. The paper explicitly states that the first-stage loss produced almost no SiO2 or SiC; therefore, this excerpt does not support the conclusion that silicone decomposes directly to a white silica residue. It reports residue characteristics for a filled/cured phenyl RTV system, not definitive behavior of pure VMQ/PDMS in argon.


---

## pqac-00000002

From text 'he2018howthecrosslinking pages 3-7'.

Chen He, Boqian Li, Ying-Ke Ren, Wu Lu, Yibing Zeng, Wei‐dong He, and Anchao Feng. How the crosslinking agent influences the thermal stability of rtv phenyl silicone rubber. Materials, 12:88, Dec 2018. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/ma12010088, doi:10.3390/ma12010088. This article has 60 citations.

The excerpt reports thermogravimetric behavior for phenyl RTV silicone rubber in nitrogen, an inert atmosphere comparable in purpose to argon but not identical. Measurements heated samples from room temperature to 900 °C at 10 °C/min. For TEOS- and TPOS-crosslinked materials, decomposition occurred in three stages: approximately 190–320 °C, 320–480 °C, and 480–630 °C. The maximum degradation rate for TEOS occurred near 380 °C, while TPOS degraded more slowly, at about 0.36% per minute at its maximum. Polysilazane-crosslinked rubber showed two stages, approximately 190–320 °C and 480–630 °C, with its maximum degradation rate shifted to about 580 °C; the study concludes that polysilazane slows thermal degradation. All formulations retained approximately 26% residue in the TG test. FT-IR and ablation observations indicate loss of C–H and Si–CH3 groups and increasing O–H and Si–O signals, attributed to polysiloxane-chain pyrolysis and formation of amorphous SiO2 and amorphous Si–O–C ceramics. However, the excerpt does not establish that the residue is white, does not provide direct visual characterization of silica color, and concerns phenyl silicone rather than generic VMQ/PDMS. Its ablation tests involve air/oxidative conditions and should not be conflated with inert-atmosphere pyrolysis.


---

## pqac-00000003

From text 'rybinski2015influenceofcenosphere pages 4-5'.

Przemysław Rybiński, Witold Żukowski, and Dariusz Bradło. Influence of cenosphere particles on thermal properties composites of silicon rubber. Journal of Thermal Analysis and Calorimetry, 122:1307-1318, Jun 2015. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10973-015-4829-0, doi:10.1007/s10973-015-4829-0. This article has 27 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt reports inert-atmosphere behavior under nitrogen, not specifically argon. For silicone rubber (VMQ/PDMS), thermogravimetry in nitrogen shows a single-stage decomposition beginning at approximately 415 °C, with the maximum mass-loss rate at 483 °C (22.85% min−1). The degradation mechanism can involve depolymerization and formation of volatile, low-molecular-mass cyclic siloxanes; cyclic compounds formed during degradation may undergo further decomposition above 450 °C. The text explains that terminal functional groups and impurities affect the mechanism: inert terminal groups favor random-chain degradation, while silanol groups can promote zip-fastener depolymerization. The excerpt does not provide a numerical upper decomposition limit, a quantified final residue, or an elemental/compositional analysis of the residue under nitrogen or argon. It also does not establish that silicone decomposes to a white silica residue. In fact, the stated products in the relevant inert-atmosphere discussion are volatile cyclic siloxane compounds. Any silica-rich residue would require evidence from additional sections or a separate residue analysis, especially because silica formation is more commonly associated with oxidative or post-pyrolysis conditions than with the reported nitrogen decomposition data.


---

## pqac-00000004

From text 'he2018howthecrosslinking pages 1-3'.

Chen He, Boqian Li, Ying-Ke Ren, Wu Lu, Yibing Zeng, Wei‐dong He, and Anchao Feng. How the crosslinking agent influences the thermal stability of rtv phenyl silicone rubber. Materials, 12:88, Dec 2018. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/ma12010088, doi:10.3390/ma12010088. This article has 60 citations.

The excerpt provides qualitative information about silicone-rubber decomposition in inert conditions but does not report the requested numerical temperature limits or a definitive residue composition. It identifies three general degradation pathways for methyl silicone rubber—unzipping, random scission, and externally catalyzed degradation. In the unzipping pathway, hydroxyl end groups initiate back-biting reactions and produce cyclic oligomers; prior pyGC-MS work is cited as finding methyl and methyl-phenyl cyclic oligomers during pyrolysis. For RTV phenyl silicone rubber, residual Si–OH groups are described as initiating polysiloxane-chain degradation through an unzipping mechanism. Phenyl silicone rubber is reported to have better thermal stability and a higher post-ablation residue than methyl silicone rubber. However, these pages do not specify decomposition onset or completion temperatures in argon, quantify the residue yield, or establish whether the final residue is white silica. The article’s stated methods—TG, TG-MS, pyGC-MS, FT-IR, and ablation testing—were intended to determine those details later in the paper. Therefore, this excerpt alone supports formation of cyclic siloxane products and enhanced residue for phenyl-containing material, but it cannot confirm the temperature range or whether VMQ/PDMS decomposes completely to white SiO2.


---

## pqac-00000005

From text 'rybinski2019impactofbasalt pages 3-5'.

Przemysław Rybiński, Bartłomiej Syrek, Witold Żukowski, and Dariusz Bradło. Impact of basalt filler and ceramizable additives on the toxicity of gaseous products emitted from thermal decomposition of silicone rubber composites. Materials, 12:3478, Oct 2019. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/ma12213478, doi:10.3390/ma12213478. This article has 10 citations.

This excerpt does not provide results for thermal decomposition of VMQ/PDMS in an inert argon atmosphere. The experiments used air as the fluidising gas, explicitly creating oxidising conditions, so the reported products cannot be directly interpreted as the products of pyrolysis under argon. The tested material was methyl vinyl silicone rubber, and gaseous products were examined at 500, 600, 700, and 800 °C. The analytical method targeted water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides, nitrous oxide, ammonia, methane, several hydrocarbons, formaldehyde, acetaldehyde, hydrogen cyanide, and cyclic siloxanes D3, D4, and D5. The excerpt describes gas analysis but does not report the solid residue’s color, composition, morphology, or silica yield. Therefore, it does not establish whether silicone decomposes to a white silica residue. It only states that the composites included silica and other inorganic fillers in some formulations; that should not be confused with silica formed from neat silicone decomposition. Evidence about residue formation or white SiO2 under argon would need to come from another section or a separate inert-atmosphere study.


---

## pqac-00000006

From text 'macfarlane1976thethermaldecomposition pages 91-96'.

The excerpt describes thermal degradation of PDMS/silicone rubber primarily as formation of volatile cyclic siloxanes. ## pqac-00000010

From text 'spirig2007anewgeneration pages 74-78'.

JV Spirig. A new generation of high temperature oxygen sensors. Unknown journal, 2007.

The excerpt describes recovery and artifact discrimination for a sealed zirconia-based Nernst oxygen sensor, but it does not explicitly report behavior after a complete power interruption. During thermal cycling, the seal showed no evidence of leakage over eight days, and repeated 48-hour cycles produced air-background voltages within 1% of prior values. At 800°C, however, the glass seal eventually softened and became a semipermeable barrier after about 40 hours, allowing oxygen exchange and compromising the internal reference pressure. After cooling to 700°C, the sensor recovered: a 55.5 mV signal indicated restoration of internal equilibrium within approximately 40 minutes. Apparent drift can be an electrochemical measurement artifact rather than a physical leak. In low-impedance mode, the measuring instrument’s bias current pumps oxygen into or out of the small sensor volume, producing baseline drift, especially for Ni/NiO and Ru/RuO2 references. Testing at high input impedance (>10 GΩ) substantially reduced this effect; a Ni/NiO sensor showed no noticeable drift over 24 hours in air. To distinguish a real leak from artifact, compare repeated thermal-cycle backgrounds, change the measurement impedance, monitor recovery after cooling, and assess whether the metal/metal-oxide reference can re-establish equilibrium through brief electrochemical treatment.

Abstract:
This work provides an overview of the aluminum (Al) recycling process, from the scrap upgrading to the melting process. Innovations and new trends regarding the Al recycling technologies are highlighted. Aluminum recycling offers advantages in terms of environmental and economic benefits. The presence of deleterious impurities in recycled Al alloys is increasing and this is the main drawback if compared to primary alloys. The continuous growth of undesired elements can be mitigated by different technologies, preliminary operations and treatments, and by the optimization of the melting process. Downgrading and dilution are possible solutions to reduce the rate of impurities, but they are not sustainable if the final use of Al alloy continuously increases. The main objectives in the development of the Al recycling are shown and discussed. In particular, the evolution of preliminary treatments of the scrap, as sorting, comminution and de-coating, is reported and a review of the melting technologies is also presented. However, the choice of performing preliminary operations to the melting stage, thus improving the operating conditions during the furnace running, is a trade-off between costs and process efficiency.

Achieving lightweight, high-strength, and biocompatible composites is a crucial objective in the field of tissue engineering. Intricate porous metallic structures, such as lattices, scaffolds, or triply periodic minimal surfaces (TPMSs), created via the selective laser melting (SLM) technique, are utilized as load-bearing matrices for filled ceramics. The primary metal alloys in this category are titanium-based Ti6Al4V and iron-based 316L, which can have either a uniform cell or a gradient structure. Well-known ceramics used in biomaterial applications include titanium dioxide (TiO2), zirconium dioxide (ZrO2), aluminum oxide (Al2O3), hydroxyapatite (HA), wollastonite (W), and tricalcium phosphate (TCP). To fill the structures fabricated by SLM, an appropriate ceramic is employed through the spark plasma sintering (SPS) method, making them suitable for in vitro or in vivo applications following minor post-processing. The combined SLM-SPS approach offers advantages, such as rapid design and prototyping, as well as assured densification and consolidation, although challenges persist in terms of large-scale structure and molding design. The individual or combined application of SLM and SPS processes can be implemented based on the specific requirements for fabricated sample size, shape complexity, densification, and mass productivity. This flexibility is a notable advantage offered by the combined processes of SLM and SPS. The present article provides an overview of metal–ceramic composites produced through SLM-SPS techniques. Mg-W-HA demonstrates promise for load-bearing biomedical applications, while Cu-TiO2-Ag exhibits potential for virucidal activities. Moreover, a functionally graded lattice (FGL) structure, either in radial or longitudinal directions, offers enhanced advantages by allowing adjustability and control over porosity, roughness, strength, and material proportions within the composite.

## pqac-00000013

From text 'li2018heattransferof pages 6-9'.

MingXing Li, HaiPeng Wang, Na Yan, and BingBo Wei. Heat transfer of micro-droplet during free fall in drop tube. Science China Technological Sciences, 61:1021-1030, May 2018. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11431-018-9240-x, doi:10.1007/s11431-018-9240-x. This article has 26 citations.

The excerpt provides useful inputs and trends for estimating heat transfer from molten metallic droplets falling through a gas, although it does not explicitly report a heat-transfer coefficient, solidification time, or Biot number. Argon is listed with thermal conductivity 0.0284 W m−1 K−1, density 599.45 × 10−3 kg m−3, viscosity 3.5864 × 10−5 Pa s, specific heat 520 J kg−1 K−1, and Prandtl number 0.65639. The article states that a Newtonian heat-transfer formulation coupled with classical heat conduction is used, so a calculated coefficient would require an appropriate forced-convection correlation based on droplet diameter, velocity, gas properties, and temperature. For size dependence, smaller droplets cool substantially faster: Ti droplets of 50 μm in He can reach approximately 4 × 10^5 K s−1, whereas 1000 μm droplets cool at approximately 10^3 K s−1. The maximum internal temperature gradient decreases from 1210 to 10.4 K mm−1 over that size range, indicating increasing internal thermal resistance in larger droplets. Metal properties needed for transient cooling or solidification calculations include density, heat capacity, thermal conductivity, and melting temperature; the excerpt tabulates these for Al, Fe, Ti, and Zr.

## pqac-00000014

From text 'li2018heattransferof pages 1-2'.

MingXing Li, HaiPeng Wang, Na Yan, and BingBo Wei. Heat transfer of micro-droplet during free fall in drop tube. Science China Technological Sciences, 61:1021-1030, May 2018. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11431-018-9240-x, doi:10.1007/s11431-018-9240-x. This article has 26 citations.

The excerpt is relevant to estimating cooling of molten-metal droplets falling through argon or another inert gas, but it does not provide a specific numerical heat-transfer coefficient, solidification-time formula, or Biot-number value. The article models droplet heat transfer by coupling a Newtonian convective heat-transfer formulation with the classical internal heat-conduction equation and solves the transient temperature field using an implicit-Euler finite-difference method. It explicitly examines the effects of liquid-metal properties, cooling-gas properties, and droplet size on cooling rate and temperature difference. For falling droplets, the surrounding-gas interaction is characterized through the Reynolds number, Re = rho_g D v_d / mu_g, with a stated drag-coefficient correlation applicable for 0.1 < Re < 4000; this helps determine falling velocity and residual acceleration but is not itself the thermal heat-transfer coefficient. The text warns that assuming a spatially uniform droplet temperature becomes unreliable for larger droplets or higher cooling rates, because internal temperature gradients become important. Thus, Biot-number-style lumped-capacitance treatment may be appropriate only when internal conduction is sufficiently rapid relative to gas-side convection; the excerpt supports evaluating this issue but does not state the required h, thermal conductivity, or critical Biot criterion. Solidification time likewise requires solving the transient thermal history together with nucleation, recalescence, and phase-growth effects.

## pqac-00000015

From text 'li2018heattransferof pages 3-5'.

MingXing Li, HaiPeng Wang, Na Yan, and BingBo Wei. Heat transfer of micro-droplet during free fall in drop tube. Science China Technological Sciences, 61:1021-1030, May 2018. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11431-018-9240-x, doi:10.1007/s11431-018-9240-x. This article has 26 citations.

The excerpt models heat transfer from spherical molten-metal droplets during free fall through gases such as argon and helium. The external convective heat-transfer coefficient is obtained from the Ranz–Marshall correlation, using gas thermal conductivity, Prandtl number, Reynolds number, and droplet diameter; radiation at the droplet surface is also included. The droplets are treated as rigid spheres with one-dimensional radial heat conduction, and the temperature field is solved numerically using an implicit finite-difference scheme. The calculation uses 500 spatial divisions and a time step of 10^-5 s. Results indicate that cooling is initially very rapid: for a 1000 μm Ti droplet, the cooling rate is approximately 2000 K s−1 before decreasing. Strong internal temperature gradients develop because heat cannot immediately conduct from the center to the surface. For motion in argon, a 200 μm droplet has a reported falling time of 1.943 s, compared with 0.763 s in vacuum. The excerpt does not provide an explicit Biot-number calculation or a general solidification-time table for different droplet sizes, although it supplies the transient temperature, cooling-rate, and center-to-surface temperature-difference framework needed for such analyses.

## pqac-00000016

From text 'li2018heattransferof pages 2-3'.

MingXing Li, HaiPeng Wang, Na Yan, and BingBo Wei. Heat transfer of micro-droplet during free fall in drop tube. Science China Technological Sciences, 61:1021-1030, May 2018. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11431-018-9240-x, doi:10.1007/s11431-018-9240-x. This article has 26 citations.

The excerpt provides a coupled transient heat-transfer framework for molten metallic droplets falling through an inert gas such as argon. Gas drag affects the falling velocity and residual acceleration, while cooling occurs through both convection and radiation at the droplet surface. The convective heat-transfer coefficient h is determined using the Ranz–Marshall correlation, although the actual correlation expression and its required dimensionless inputs are not included in this excerpt. Instead of assuming a spatially uniform droplet temperature, the paper solves the spherical heat-conduction equation within the droplet, using the liquid metal specific heat and thermal conductivity. The initial droplet temperature is specified as T0, and the surface boundary condition combines convective cooling, h[T(R,t)−Tg], with radiative exchange proportional to [T(R,t)^4−Tg^4]. Symmetry requires a zero temperature gradient at the droplet center. This model can be used to calculate cooling histories and solidification times for different droplet radii by changing R and solving until the relevant solidification temperature or phase-change criterion is reached. The excerpt does not provide numerical h values, explicit solidification times, Biot-number calculations, or material/property data. A Biot number would generally be used to assess whether internal conduction resistance is negligible, but the text specifically notes that the uniform-temperature approximation becomes unreliable as droplet size and cooling rate increase.
